title: Honeybees in trouble
passageHtml:
READING PASSAGE 1

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1–14, which are based on Reading Passage 1 below.

Honeybees in trouble

Can native pollinators fill the gap?

A A Recently, ominous headlines have described a mysterious ailment, colony collapse disorder (CCD), which is wiping out the honeybees that pollinate many crops. Without honeybees, the story goes, fields will be sterile, economies will collapse, and food will be scarce.

B B ‘Clean farming’ techniques including removing natural plant life from the edges of fields and the sides of roadways, the widespread use of organophosphates in pesticides, and planting monocultural crops on a broad scale have emerged at the same time. This has made farmland hostile to bees, and has killed many, since bees are just as susceptible to poison as other insects or pests. Rachel Carson warned about exactly this in her 1962 environmentalist landmark Silent Spring, raising the alarm about these approaches to agriculture and warning that the absence of pollinators could create a ‘Fruitless Fall’.

C C As pollinators disappeared from the wild, the honeybee has emerged as a savior, offering farms hope and having so far prevented the ‘Fruitless Fall’. The biology of this bee is particularly well matched to the new system of agriculture that has emerged, and while honeybees have been semidomesticated for thousands of years, dating back to ancient Egypt, the familiarity is not the main reason for their new relevance. When insecticides are spread in a particular field, the hives of honeybees can be shuttered and transported. Different types of crops can be pollinated by honeybees, since they are generalists. As many as 20000 to 100000 bees live in each hive, so while they are not the most efficient for every crop, they make up for this with volume of output. The US. Department of Agriculture's Jim Cane says that ‘the honeybee is the one bee you would want for farming, no doubt about it.’ Contemporary industrial agriculture has created an important job for the honeybee to do. More kinds of food are grown and delivered to more locations at a lower expense under industrial agriculture than that has ever been possible before. When you turn photosynthesis into some sort of automated process, however, and turn an entire continent into an assembly line, you strip out some of the important natural resilience of native ecosystems and leave them vulnerable.

D D This level of specialization is functional when everything else is at equilibrium but can turn swiftly to extinction if the system loses balance, making it a dangerous enterprise, according to agronomist Breno Freitas. Human beings run the risk of becoming overspecialized by creating a system of farming that relies so completely on just one species for pollination. The vulnerability of industrial agriculture is revealed when the link between the honeybee and humankind is damaged, as is the case with colony collapse disorder.

E E Crop pollination can be performed by wild bees as well, and some of them are being managed quite successfully. Jim Cane says ‘the key is to service crops in just a few years using native bees in sufficient quantities with steady reliability. Many crops will need to see, in just twotothree weeks or less, millions of flowers pollinated per acre.’ Since honeybees are less efficient at pollinating than native bees for certain crops, fewer native bees will be required to complete the task. 50000 to 150000 honeybees would be required to pollinate one hectare of almonds or apples, but just 750 Osmia lignaria, or blue orchard bees, can cover the same area. Similar work is being done across the globe by other bee tinkerers. A native pollinator of wild cashews, Centris tarsata, can thrive in Brazilian commercial cashew fields if given a source of floral oils, such as those provided by interplanting cashews with Caribbean cherry trees, according to Breno Freitas.

F F In certain places, native bees may already be doing more than they're getting credit for. Ecologist Rachael Winfree recently led a team that looked at pollination of four summer crops (tomato, watermelon, peppers, and muskmelon) at 29 farms in the region of New Jersey and Pennsylvania. Winfree's team identified 54 species of wild bees that visited these crops and found that wild bees were the most important pollinators in the system: even though managed honeybees were present on many of the farms, wild bees were responsible for 62 percent of flower visits in the study. In another study focusing specifically on watermelon, Winfree and her colleagues calculated that native bees alone could provide sufficient pollination at 90 percent of the 23 farms studied. By contrast, honeybees alone could provide pollination at only 78 percent of farms.

G G ‘The region I work in is not a typical area where most food is produced,’ Winfree admits. In the Delaware Valley, most farms and farm fields are relatively small, each farmer typically grows a variety of crops, and farms are interspersed with suburbs and other types of land use which means there are opportunities for homeowners to get involved in bee conservation, too. The landscape is a beefriendly patchwork that provides a variety of nesting habitats and floral resources distributed among different kinds of crops, weedy field margins, fallow fields, suburban neighborhoods, and semi natural habitats like old woodlots, all at a relatively small scale. In other words, ‘pollinatorfriendly’ farming practices would not only aid pollination of agricultural crops, but also serve as a key element in the overall conservation strategy for wild pollinators, and often aid other wild species as well.

H H Of course, not all farmers will be able to implement all of these practices. And researchers are suggesting a shift to a kind of polyglot agricultural system. For some smallscale farms, native bees may indeed be all that is needed. For larger operations, a suite of managed bees—with honeybees filling the generalist role and other native bees pollinating specific crops—could be augmented by free pollination services from resurgent wild pollinators. In other words, they are saying, we still have an opportunity to replace a risky monoculture with something diverse, resilient, and robust.

Questions 1–5

Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in Reading Passage 1?

Choose

YESif the statement agrees with the claims of the writer
NOif the statement contradicts the claims of the writer
NOT GIVENif it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this

1 Clean farming practices would be harmful to bees.

2 In the United States, farmers have used honeybees in a large scale over the past few years.

3 Human beings started to domesticate honeybees since the 1900s.

4 The blue orchard bee is the most efficient pollinator among native bees for every crop.

5 It is beneficial to other species when wild bees are protected.

Questions 6–9

Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

6 The example of the ‘Fruitless Fall’ underlines the writer's point about

7 The writer mentions factories and assembly lines to illustrate

8 In paragraph F, Winfree's experiment proves that

9 What does the writer want to suggest in the last paragraph?

Questions 10–14

Complete each sentence with the correct ending A-F below.

10 Headline of colony collapse disorder states that

11 Viewpoints of Freitas manifest that

12 Examples of blue orchard bees have shown that

13 Centris tarsata is mentioned to exemplify that

14 One finding of the research in Delaware Valley is that

A native pollinators can survive when a specific plant is supplied.
B the absence of the honeybees would cause severe consequences both to commerce and agriculture.
C honey bees cannot be bred.
D some agricultural landscapes are favorable for supporting wild bees.
E large numbers of honey bees are needed to pollinate certain types of crops.
F an agricultural system is fragile when relying on a single pollinator.
